objectClass.primaryType: machinist bench vise with swivel base
objectClass.notes: Bare ferrous metal workholding clamp, bilaterally symmetric about the vertical plane containing the screw axis. Four macro assemblies: swivel base, body casting with the fixed jaw, movable jaw on a slide bar, lead screw with a ball-ended T-handle. Two real kinematic degrees of freedom are visible in the reference: the jaw translates along the screw axis and the whole body swivels about the base axis; the handle bar slides and the screw rotates. No paint, no decal, no dielectric surface anywhere.

reasoning: Silhouette is interrupted at three places by real negative space (the jaw gap, the gap under the exposed screw run, the gap between base lobes) — a single hull cannot produce it.
Four macro assemblies decompose into ~16 visible sub-parts; the movable jaw alone is arm + slide bar + thrust lobe + jaw plate.
Hierarchy is genuinely three deep: base -> body -> fixed jaw arm -> jaw plate -> serration row.
Repetition is dense and identity-defining: two helical thread runs (~29 visible turns combined), an axial knurl band, two serration rows, four base lobes, four hex fasteners.
Four distinct machining finishes share one metal family: rough casting, machined stock, dark-oxide screw, near-polished handle.
Occlusion risk is moderate: the entire rear half, the base underside and both internal channels are unseen and reconstructed by symmetry/convention.
Action readiness is high — the reference object is a mechanism, so jaw travel, body swivel, screw spin and handle slide all need real pivots and limits.

specDepthDecision.rationale: Chosen from the observed structure: multi-assembly mechanism, dense helical/knurl/serration repetition, four finish variants of one metal family, and two real kinematic axes. Not ultra-complex: there is no organic surface, no pattern finish, no wear layer and no text/marking to match.

details.note: Horizontal rows of triangular gripping teeth across both jaw faces; teeth run across the jaw width, plate stands proud of the arm.
Each jaw plate carries a small stepped tab standing above the arm's top edge — a strong silhouette cue at the top of the jaw gap.
Trapezoidal (acme) thread, two exposed runs: a long run between body face and movable jaw, a short tail past the -X body face. Crest line is the brightest specular in that zone.
Fine axial knurl ridges around the thrust ring between the movable jaw lobe and the handle; reads as a dense vertical hatch.
Every casting edge is filleted, never sharp; the inner scallop of each jaw arm meets its top face through a broad fillet.
The body's top plateau behind the fixed jaw is bounded by a hard chamfer that catches a bright grazing rim line.
Both exposed screw ends are chamfered rather than square-cut.
Hex bolt heads seated in the front base lobes; hexagonal head, raised, machined finish brighter than the casting around it.
Single hex-headed swivel lock bolt on the front of the swivel collar.
Small hex fastener boss on the lower front face of the body casting near the swivel.
Through mounting holes centred in each radial base lobe; counterbored mouth.
A crisp circular parting seam separates the swivel collar from the fixed foot disc — a recessed groove plus a darker crevice, not a painted line.
The slide bar exits the body through a rectangular guide mouth; the gap around it reads as a dark recessed seam.
The two handle balls carry the tightest, brightest specular lobes in the reference — the lowest roughness in the whole object.
Low-amplitude mottled roughness/tone variation over every cast surface (sand-cast grain), absent from machined and turned surfaces.

definitionOfDone: Rendered silhouette reproduces the reference's three negative spaces: the jaw gap, the gap beneath the exposed mid screw run, and the gaps between base lobes.
Both jaw arms show the hooked profile — convex outer face, deep concave inner scallop, broad fillet at the top — not a plain rectangular upright.
Two separate exposed thread runs are present with visible helical relief, not a smooth cylinder and not a texture.
Longitudinal proportions match the reference: overall width : height ~2.25:1, base disc diameter ~0.42 x overall width, jaw opening ~0.17 x overall width.
Four finish variants of one metal family are distinguishable in the render: rough casting, machined stock, dark-oxide screw, near-polished handle.
The T-handle reads as a straight bar with a sphere at each end, cross-drilled through the screw head and free to slide.
Model is explodable and clickable, and the two real kinematic axes (jaw travel, body swivel) are driveable with limits.

assumptions: Rear (-Z) half of every casting is reconstructed by mirroring the observed +Z half; it is inference, not observation.
Base underside, nut-boss interior and slide-channel interior are built to engineering convention because they are never visible in the reference.
Jaw-plate serration pitch is set to 0.022 units and tooth depth to 0.014; the reference pitch is below reliable count resolution.
The chamfered body plateau is modelled as a true flat anvil pad; the reference cannot distinguish that from a plain cast chamfer.
All four base lobes carry fasteners; only the two front lobes are observed.
Absolute scale is a convention: a 102 mm jaw width, expressed as 1 unit = 100 mm. The reference carries no scale cue.
Thread pitch is set to 0.068 units, counted from the reference with about +/-2 turns of uncertainty across the long run.
Base lobes are placed on the 45-degree diagonals; the side view fixes their longitudinal extent but not their azimuth, and a square four-bolt pattern is the convention.
The reference is available to agent vision only, as a conversation attachment, so PBR channel values are observation-derived rather than extracted from pixels.

proceduralStrategy: Block out the macro silhouette from measured landmark positions, not from a guessed bounding box.
Author each casting as an extruded side outline: the outline is what carries the identity, and a box stack loses the chamfers and the concave scallop.
Revolve everything concentric with an axis (collar, bosses, thrust ring, screw core, handle) so it stays circular from every azimuth.
Sweep the thread as a helical spine — no revolve or extrude can produce a ridge that advances while it winds.
Build teeth, knurl and lobes as geometry wherever they break a silhouette edge; use material response only for what does not.
Separate the four machining finishes by roughness and its variation, never by albedo.
Keep every deterministic procedural field seeded so a rebuild is byte-identical.
